summaries.summary: Performance appraisal (PA) is an important HR process that periodically measures employee performance, links organizational goals to daily activities, and is actively researched.

Modern PA systems record interactions in computer-readable databases, enabling automated statistical, data-mining and text-mining analysis for large organizations with thousands of distributed employees.
A typical PA process involves multi-step multi-modal communication through self-appraisal, supervisor assessment, and peer feedback, with several business questions of interest to managers.
The paper develops text mining techniques for HR executives requiring minimum training data and parameter experimentation, implemented in a PA system at a large multi-national IT company.
The paper is organized around related work, the PA dataset, sentence classification, attribute mapping, peer feedback summarization, conclusions, and further work.
Related work on sentence classification includes SVM and other classifiers for biomedical abstracts, emails, message boards, legal documents, and unsupervised linguistic patterns.
The paper notes related work on dialogue acts but does not review it, citing Cotterill BIBREF17 on classifying email questions into dialogue acts.
Little work exists on mining performance appraisals data, including sentence classification, goal-description matching, and label propagation for discovering aspects in supervisor assessments.

The paper used supervisor assessment and peer feedback text from performance appraisals of 4528 employees, with 26972 supervisor assessment sentences and word-count statistics min:4 max:217 average:15.5 STDEV:9.2 Q1:9 Q2:14 Q3:19.
The paper focuses on three PA sentence classes: STRENGTH, WEAKNESS, and SUGGESTION, noting overlap between WEAKNESS and SUGGESTION and giving examples.

The authors describe linguistic aspects of STRENGTH, WEAKNESS, and SUGGESTION sentences and build POS-tagged pattern-based unsupervised classifiers with tie-breaking rules.
They randomly selected 2000 sentences as dataset D1, with 705 STRENGTH, 103 WEAKNESS, 822 SUGGESTION, and 370 OTHER labels, and trained several multi-class classifiers using 5-fold cross-validation.
Using TextBlob polarity scores as a sentiment baseline showed similar positive and negative sentiment distributions in STRENGTH and SUGGESTION, making sentiment information not much useful.
From 12742 predicted STRENGTH sentences and 9160 WEAKNESS or SUGGESTION sentences, noun clusters and sentence clusters were compared, with users finding noun clusters more meaningful.
PA can be done along predefined attributes, and HR managers defined 15 attributes, including FUNCTIONAL_EXCELLENCE covering software engineering life-cycle tasks and technologies.
Mapping each sentence in the 3 classes to zero, one, two or more attributes is a multi-class multi-label classification problem.
The same 2000 sentences in Dataset D1 were manually tagged with attributes as dataset D2, with specified label counts and 321, 1070, 470 and 139 sentences having 0, 1, 2, or more than 2 attributes.
Precision, Recall and F-measure for multi-label classification are computed using predicted and actual label sets for each instance.
Undefined instance-level precision or recall cases are excluded from averaging, and overall F-measure is computed using overall precision and recall.
The PA system includes peer feedback comments for each employee, and answering the third question requires creating a summary of all comments about a given employee.
Peer comment sentences are identified and POS-tagged, candidate phrases are extracted, and Integer Linear Programming (ILP) selects a subset as the final summary.

Various parameters are used to evaluate a candidate phrase for its importance.
A complete list of parameters is described in detail in Table TABREF36.
ILP constraints limit selected phrases, ensure leadership attribute coverage, prevent shared headwords, restrict single-word phrases, and use soft constraints with slack-variable penalties.
The objective function maximizes total importance score of selected candidate phrases while minimizing the sum of all slack variables.

On a dataset of 100 employees, ILP-based summaries were compared with manual summaries using ROUGE unigram score and Sumy algorithms, showing comparable performance and human preference for phrase-based summaries.

The paper analyzed PA text using sentence classification, clustering, multi-class multi-label classification, and ILP-based peer feedback summarization, with SVM with ADWS kernel BIBREF18 and Logistic Regression performing best.

Further work includes comparing and combining insights from structured data and unstructured text, and automatically discovering additional performance attributes beyond the 15 attributes currently used by HR.
